title: Storing a value
prompt:
You run this line and nothing appears in the output.

```r
weight_kg <- 70
```

What happened?

options.text: R stored the value and had nothing to report
options.feedback:
Right. `<-` means *put this value in this name*. Storing something
isn't a question, so R has no answer to print. Type `weight_kg` on
its own line and you'll see the 70 come back.

It worked. R only prints when you ask it a question — `70 + 5` is a
question, `weight_kg <- 70` is an instruction. Instructions don't
produce output.

options.text: You have to print it before R will store it
options.feedback:
The value is already stored. Printing and storing are separate
things: `<-` stores, and typing the name on its own line shows you
what's there.

title: Using what you stored
prompt:
A patient weighs 70 kg and is 1.75 m tall. Two values are already stored
for you as variables. Add a line that calculates their BMI.

BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in m × height in m)
hint: You can use a variable anywhere you'd use the number itself.

solution.why:
Once a value has been named as a variable, R substitutes that value
wherever the variable name appears. The parentheses matter for the
same reason they did with the three temperatures.

checks.on_fail:
Not 22.86 yet. Check that the height is squared before the division
happens.

misconceptions.feedback:
Without parentheses R divides 70 by 1.75 and then multiplies the
result by 1.75 again, landing you straight back at the weight.
Wrap the whole denominator.

That gives the right answer, but you've typed the numbers in
directly. Use the variables instead — that's the point of storing
them. If the patient's weight changes, you want to change it in one
place rather than hunting through the whole script.

title: Reusing a name
prompt:
What does this print?

```r
dose_mg <- 500
dose_mg <- 250
dose_mg
```
hint: R runs the lines in order, top to bottom.

options.feedback:
Right. The second line replaces the first. R keeps no history and
gives no warning — the 500 is simply gone. This is worth
remembering when you run parts of a script out of order, which is
how a name ends up holding something you didn't expect.

The second assignment overwrites the first. R works through the
lines in order, so by the time it reaches the third line the name
holds 250.

A name holds one value at a time. Storing something new replaces
what was there.

options.text: An error — the name is already taken
options.feedback:
R lets you reuse a name freely, without comment. Convenient, and
occasionally the reason a number is wrong.

Right. `Weight` and `weight` are two different names as far as R is
concerned — capital letters count. This is one of the few errors
that says exactly what's wrong, so it's worth learning to read now:
object not found means the name doesn't exist, usually because of a
typo or a line that never ran.

options.text: `140` — R matches the name closely enough
options.feedback:
R never guesses at names. `Weight` and `weight` are as different to
R as `weight` and `height`.

This one is an error, not a warning, and the difference matters: a
warning lets R carry on and hand you an answer, while an error
stops it in its tracks. R can't continue without knowing what
`weight` refers to, so nothing is returned at all.

title: Numbers in quotes
hint: The quotes change what kind of thing the 5 is.

options.text: An error about a non-numeric argument
options.feedback:
Right. Quotes make something *text*, even when what's inside looks
like a number. R won't do arithmetic on text, and it won't quietly
convert it for you either. The error mentions a non-numeric
argument, which is R's way of saying one of these two things isn't
a number.

options.text: `6` — R converts the text to a number
options.feedback:
Some languages do exactly that. R doesn't, and that's a mercy:
silent conversion is how a column of lab values turns into
nonsense without anyone noticing.

That's what `+` does in some other languages. In R, `+` only ever
means arithmetic, so it refuses rather than improvising.

title: Asking what something is
prompt:
R has a function called `class()` that tells you what kind of thing a
value is. Use it to check `4.5`.
hint: The function name goes directly before the opening bracket.

solution.why:
`class()` reports what kind of value it was handed. It's the fastest
way to check whether something is a number, text, or something else
when arithmetic is failing and you can't see why.

checks.on_fail:
That didn't return the word "numeric". Try the function named after
what class of thing a value belongs to.

misconceptions.feedback:
`typeof()` is a close relative and it does work, but it reports how
R stores the value internally rather than what kind of thing it is.
`class()` is the one you'll want day to day.

title: Comparisons make a third kind of value
prompt:
What does this return?

```r
sbp <- 118
sbp > 140
```
hint: The answer isn't a number and it isn't text.

options.feedback:
Right. A comparison returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` — a third kind of
value, called logical. You'll rely on this constantly once you
start filtering data: the question "which rows have a systolic over
140" is answered as a long run of TRUEs and FALSEs.

Close in spirit — R will treat `FALSE` as 0 if you do arithmetic on
it — but what comes back is the word `FALSE`, not the number.

options.text: An error, because 118 is not greater than 140
options.feedback:
A comparison that turns out to be false isn't an error. R is
answering your question, and the answer is no.

title: Adding up TRUEs
prompt:
What does this return?

```r
TRUE + TRUE
```
hint:
R is willing to do arithmetic here, which tells you something about how
it stores TRUE and FALSE.

options.feedback:
Yes. When arithmetic is involved, R treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE`
as 0. This looks like a curiosity and turns out to be useful: once
you can ask a question of every row at once, adding up the answers
counts how many rows said yes.

options.text: An error — you can't add words
options.feedback:
`TRUE` isn't a word, it's a logical value, and R is happy to
convert it to a number when the situation calls for one. Contrast
that with `\"5\" + 1`, which it refuses outright.

That would make sense if `+` meant something like "and". It
doesn't — `+` is always arithmetic, so R converts both values to
numbers first.

title: Why won't this run?
prompt:
This was meant to calculate a mean arterial pressure, but it fails with
an error about a non-numeric argument. Click the part that causes it.
hint:
Everything here is spelled correctly and every parenthesis matches. The
problem is what kind of value one of these is.

options.feedback:
Right. The quotes make this text rather than a number, so the
arithmetic on the third line has nothing to work with. Notice how
little there was to see — one pair of quotation marks, and nothing
else about the code looks wrong.

This one is a proper number, no quotes. Compare it to the line
above and the difference should stand out.

This is the line that *reports* the error, but it isn't the cause.
The formula is correct. It's being handed something it can't use,
and that came from further up.

title: Fix the types
prompt:
Press **Run** first and read what R tells you. It's one of the messages
you'll see most often, and it's worth recognising on sight.

Then fix the two assignments so the calculation runs and returns the mean
arterial pressure.
hint:
Nothing about the formula needs to change. `binary operator` in the error
message means an operator with something on each side — here, the `+`.

solution.why:
Dropping the quotes makes these numbers rather than text, and the
arithmetic works. When the values come from a spreadsheet rather than
your keyboard you can't just delete the quotes, and then `as.numeric()`
does the same job — but the check you run is the same either way.

checks.on_fail:
Not 93.33 yet. Both values need to be numbers before the formula
can use them.

misconceptions.feedback:
The systolic is still in quotes, so it's still text. R won't
convert it for you when the arithmetic reaches it.

The diastolic is still text. Both values have to be numbers, not
just one.
